topics.title: Searching Algorithms
topics.keyConcept: Searching locates a target value in a collection. Binary Search divides sorted space log-linearly, while Interpolation Search calculates positions like looking up a dictionary.
topics.content:
Searching algorithms locate a target key within a collection of records:

  • Linear Search: Scans each element sequentially from index 0 to $n-1$. Best case is \( O(1) \) (target at index 0), worst case is \( O(n) \). No sorting required.
  • Binary Search: Divide-and-conquer on sorted lists. Compares the target with the middle element. If smaller, search the left half; if larger, search the right half. Time complexity is \( O(\log n) \).
  • Interpolation Search: An improved version of binary search for uniformly distributed sorted lists. Parallel to how we look up a name in a phonebook, it estimates the probe position using interpolation: \[ pos = low + \frac{key - arr[low]}{arr[high] - arr[low]} \cdot (high - low) \] Best case is \( O(1) \), Average case is \( O(\log \log n) \), Worst case is \( O(n) \) (when values grow exponentially, creating clusters).

Real-World Project Example: Search queries in database indices. An indexed column containing sequential ID numbers (1001, 1002, 1003, ...) is uniformly distributed; Interpolation Search locates an ID instantly in $O(\log \log n)$ time.
topics.commonMistakes: Applying Binary Search or Interpolation Search on unsorted arrays. These algorithms assume sorted order; searching on unsorted inputs yields incorrect results or infinite loops.
topics.interviewTip: In interviews, when asked about searching on sorted arrays, suggest Binary Search first. If the interviewer mentions that the values are uniformly distributed (like census data or sequential IDs), mention **Interpolation Search** and describe its \( O(\log \log n) \) average complexity to stand out.

topics.title: Merge Sort: Trace & Pseudocode
topics.keyConcept: Merge Sort is a stable, divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that guarantees O(n log n) time in all cases but requires O(n) auxiliary memory.
topics.content:
Merge Sort recursively splits the array into two halves, sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves back together. It is highly suited for sorting linked lists and large datasets too big to fit in RAM (External Sorting).

Pseudocode:

function mergeSort(arr, low, high):
    if low < high:
        mid = low + (high - low) / 2
        mergeSort(arr, low, mid)
        mergeSort(arr, mid + 1, high)
        merge(arr, low, mid, high)

function merge(arr, low, mid, high):
    // Copy elements to temp arrays L[] and R[]
    // Compare and copy back to arr in sorted order

Step-by-Step Execution Trace: Let's sort the array [12, 11, 13, 5]:

  1. Divide: Split array at mid = 1. Subproblems are [12, 11] and [13, 5].
  2. Subproblem 1: Split [12, 11] into [12] and [11]. Sort/Merge: [11, 12].
  3. Subproblem 2: Split [13, 5] into [13] and [5]. Sort/Merge: [5, 13].
  4. Final Merge: Merge [11, 12] and [5, 13].
    Compare 11 and 5 -> take 5. Array: [5].
    Compare 11 and 13 -> take 11. Array: [5, 11].
    Compare 12 and 13 -> take 12. Array: [5, 11, 12].
    Copy remaining elements -> Array: [5, 11, 12, 13].
topics.commonMistakes: Forgetting that Merge Sort requires \( O(n) \) auxiliary space to hold the temporary subarrays during the merge step. It is not an in-place sort.

topics.title: Quick Sort: Trace & Pseudocode
topics.keyConcept: Quick Sort partitions arrays around a pivot in-place, achieving O(n log n) average speed, but degrading to O(n^2) if partitions are unbalanced.
topics.content:
Quick Sort selects a 'pivot' element, partitions the array such that all elements smaller than the pivot are placed before it and all larger elements are placed after it, and recursively sorts the partitions.

Pseudocode:

function quickSort(arr, low, high):
    if low < high:
        pIndex = partition(arr, low, high)
        quickSort(arr, low, pIndex - 1)
        quickSort(arr, pIndex + 1, high)

function partition(arr, low, high):
    pivot = arr[high] // Pick last element as pivot
    i = low - 1       // Index of smaller element
    for j = low to high - 1:
        if arr[j] < pivot:
            i++
            swap(arr[i], arr[j])
    swap(arr[i + 1], arr[high])
    return i + 1

Step-by-Step Execution Trace: Sort array [10, 80, 30, 90, 40] with pivot = 40 (last element):

  1. Initialize: i = -1.
  2. j = 0: arr[0] = 10 < 40 -> i = 0, swap arr[0] and arr[0]. Array: [10, 80, 30, 90, 40].
  3. j = 1: arr[1] = 80 > 40 -> Do nothing.
  4. j = 2: arr[2] = 30 < 40 -> i = 1, swap arr[1] and arr[2]. Array: [10, 30, 80, 90, 40].
  5. j = 3: arr[3] = 90 > 40 -> Do nothing.
  6. End loop. Swap arr[i+1] (80) and pivot (40). Array: [10, 30, 40, 90, 80]. Pivot 40 is now at index 2.
  7. Recursively sort left partition [10, 30] and right partition [90, 80].
topics.commonMistakes: Not knowing that Quick Sort is an unstable sort. The swapping operations during partitioning can change the relative order of duplicate elements.
topics.interviewTip: Why does Quick Sort have a worst-case time complexity of \( O(n^2) \)? How can we prevent it? It happens on sorted input with a fixed end-pivot. Solve it by picking a random index as the pivot.

topics.title: Heap Sort: Trace & Pseudocode
topics.keyConcept: Heap Sort is an in-place, unstable O(n log n) sorting algorithm that utilizes a Max Heap binary tree representation to extract elements.
topics.content:
Heap Sort is an in-place sort using a Max Heap binary tree structure where every parent node is greater than or equal to its children. It builds a heap, swaps the root (max element) with the last leaf, and restores heap properties recursively.

Pseudocode:

function heapSort(arr):
    n = arr.length
    // Step 1: Build Max Heap
    for i = n/2 - 1 down to 0:
        heapify(arr, n, i)
    // Step 2: Extract elements
    for i = n-1 down to 1:
        swap(arr[0], arr[i])
        heapify(arr, i, 0)

function heapify(arr, size, rootIndex):
    largest = rootIndex
    left = 2 * rootIndex + 1
    right = 2 * rootIndex + 2
    if left < size and arr[left] > arr[largest]: largest = left
    if right < size and arr[right] > arr[largest]: largest = right
    if largest != rootIndex:
        swap(arr[rootIndex], arr[largest])
        heapify(arr, size, largest)

Step-by-Step Execution Trace: Sort array [4, 10, 3, 5, 1]:

  1. Build Max Heap: Heapify starts at parent index 1 (value 10). Leaves are 5, 1. No swaps needed. Next parent index 0 (value 4). Leaves are 10, 3. Swap 4 and 10. Run heapify on child index 1. Leaves are 4, 1. Swap 4 and 5. Max Heap representation is: [10, 5, 3, 4, 1].
  2. Extract Max: Swap root 10 and last element 1. Heap is [1, 5, 3, 4 | 10]. Heapify size 4. Swap 1 and 5. Swap 1 and 4. Heap: [5, 4, 3, 1 | 10].
  3. Extract Max: Swap 5 and 1. Heap is [1, 4, 3 | 5, 10]. Heapify size 3. Swap 1 and 4. Heap: [4, 1, 3 | 5, 10].
  4. Extract Max: Swap 4 and 3. Heap is [3, 1 | 4, 5, 10]. Heapify size 2. No swaps.
  5. Extract Max: Swap 3 and 1. Sorted array: [1, 3, 4, 5, 10].
topics.commonMistakes: Assuming Heap Sort is faster than Quick Sort in practice. Although both have \( O(n \log n) \) average complexity, Quick Sort has much better cache locality and lower constant factors, making it faster in actual benchmarks.

topics.title: Complexity Comparison Table
topics.keyConcept: Sorting algorithms must be selected based on time limits, memory overhead constraints, and stability requirements.
topics.content:
A summary of the efficiency of searching and sorting algorithms:

AlgorithmBest CaseAverage CaseWorst CaseAux SpaceStability
Linear Search\( O(1) \)\( O(n) \)\( O(n) \)\( O(1) \)Stable
Binary Search\( O(1) \)\( O(\log n) \)\( O(\log n) \)\( O(1) \)N/A
Interpolation Search\( O(1) \)\( O(\log \log n) \)\( O(n) \)\( O(1) \)N/A
Merge Sort\( O(n \log n) \)\( O(n \log n) \)\( O(n \log n) \)\( O(n) \)Stable
Quick Sort\( O(n \log n) \)\( O(n \log n) \)\( O(n^2) \)\( O(\log n) \) recursion stackUnstable
Heap Sort\( O(n \log n) \)\( O(n \log n) \)\( O(n \log n) \)\( O(1) \)Unstable
topics.commonMistakes: Stating that Heap Sort is stable. Because Heap Sort swaps parent and leaf elements across broad indices, duplicate values can easily change relative order, rendering the sort unstable.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the formula used by Interpolation Search to calculate the probe position?
practiceQuestions.answer: The formula is: \[ pos = low + \frac{key - arr[low]}{arr[high] - arr[low]} \cdot (high - low) \] where 'key' is the target search value, and 'low' and 'high' are the boundary indices of the current subarray.

practiceQuestions.question: Why does Quick Sort have a worst-case time complexity of \( O(n^2) \)? How can we prevent it?
practiceQuestions.answer: Quick Sort hits its worst-case \( O(n^2) \) complexity when the partition process is highly unbalanced (e.g., when the array is already sorted and we consistently pick the first or last element as the pivot). We can prevent this by using a randomized pivot (Randomized Quick Sort) or picking the median element (Median-of-Three method) to ensure balanced splits.

practiceQuestions.question: Compare Merge Sort and Heap Sort in terms of Time and Space complexity.
practiceQuestions.answer: Both Merge Sort and Heap Sort have the same time complexity of \( O(n \log n) \) in the best, average, and worst cases. However, they differ in space complexity: Merge Sort requires \( O(n) \) auxiliary space for merging arrays, while Heap Sort is an in-place algorithm requiring only \( O(1) \) auxiliary space.

practiceQuestions.question: Explain the concept of sorting algorithm stability with a quick example.
practiceQuestions.answer: A sorting algorithm is stable if it preserves the relative order of records with equal keys. For example, if we sort database entries by first name, and we have two entries 'John Smith' and 'John Adams' where John Smith originally appeared before John Adams, a stable sort guarantees that John Smith will still appear before John Adams in the sorted output.

practiceQuestions.question: What are the steps involved in Heap Sort?
practiceQuestions.answer: (1) Build a Max Heap from the input data. (2) Swap the root element (maximum value) with the last element of the heap. (3) Decrease the heap size by 1. (4) Run heapify on the root to restore the Max Heap property. (5) Repeat steps 2-4 until the heap size is 1.

mcqs.question: What is the average-case time complexity of Interpolation Search on a uniformly distributed sorted array?
mcqs.explanation: Interpolation search exhibits an average complexity of \(O(\log \log n)\) under uniform distribution, which is faster than standard binary search.

mcqs.question: Which of the following sorting algorithms is stable and has a worst-case time complexity of O(n log n)?
mcqs.explanation: Merge Sort is a stable sorting algorithm that guarantees \(O(n \log n)\) performance in all cases.

mcqs.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
mcqs.explanation: In the worst case (e.g., sorted input with first element pivot), Quick Sort splits elements into partitions of size 0 and n-1, resulting in \(O(n^2)\) performance.

mcqs.question: Which sorting algorithm is in-place and has a guaranteed worst-case time complexity of O(n log n)?
mcqs.explanation: Heap Sort sorts elements in-place (requiring \(O(1)\) space) and guarantees \(O(n \log n)\) worst-case time complexity.

mcqs.question: Under what condition does Interpolation Search degrade to its worst-case complexity of O(n)?
options: When the array is very small
When elements grow exponentially or contain large clusters
When the target key is not in the array
mcqs.explanation: If the data does not scale linearly (e.g., exponential distribution like 1, 2, 4, 8, 1024, etc.), the calculated probe positions will be highly skewed, leading to linear scans.

mcqs.question: Which of the following sorting algorithms is NOT stable?
mcqs.explanation: Heap Sort is unstable because the heap's node-swapping operations can change the relative order of duplicate elements.

mcqs.question: What is the space complexity of Merge Sort?
mcqs.explanation: Merge Sort requires an auxiliary array of size \(n\) to merge sorted subarrays together, resulting in \(O(n)\) space complexity.

mcqs.question: In the heapify operation of Heap Sort, what is the height of a node represented in time complexity terms?
mcqs.explanation: Moving an element down the heap structure takes time proportional to the height of the heap, which is bounded by \(O(\log n)\).

mcqs.question: Randomizing the pivot in Quick Sort is done to:
options: Reduce the space complexity to O(1)
Avoid the worst-case O(n^2) time complexity on sorted input
Make it faster than linear search
mcqs.explanation: Randomizing pivot choices prevents consistent worst-case partitions, keeping the expected time complexity at \(O(n \log n)\).

mcqs.question: What is the best-case time complexity of Heap Sort?
mcqs.explanation: Even if the array is already sorted, Heap Sort must still perform extraction and heapify actions, taking \(O(n \log n)\) time.
